name: Opunake Surf Reef
year: Planned for March 2006 construction start [R3]; most retrospective sources say started 2006 [R2]; one 2021 source says 2005 [R1] — disputed Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3) give construction commencing early 2006 [R13], vs 2005 per [R1]: sources disagree. UPDATE 2026-10-13 (TRC Technical Report 2009-33, Lior's copy) [R18]: the three coastal permits were granted 31 May 2005 (expiry 1 June 2018); construction began in early 2006, was halted by weather and because the equipment was needed at Mount Maunganui, and continued in the following two summers (site sign: works period February 2007 to May 200? - last digit blurred, read as 2008); as of April 2008 27 geo-textile bags were in place with fine-tuning planned for summer 2009/2010 (printed p.4); in Sept 2009 the reef was 'basically in place' but not complete [R18]. The 2021 source's '2005' may refer to the 2005 consents; construction itself started in 2006 (TRC).
type: Submerged multi-purpose reef, sand-filled geotextile ("geo-container") bags — 27 bags in place by 2009 [R2]
purpose: Increase surfable days at Opunake from an estimated 1-in-8 to 1-in-3, to draw tourism and jobs to a South Taranaki district with a slowly declining population; not designed for coastal-erosion protection [R2][R3]
size: North reef only (the larger south reef was never built). DESIGN SIZE at consent stage (TRC 2009, printed p.4) [R18]: about 99 m long x 30 m wide x 3.5 m high, plan area about 2,970 m2 (= 99 x 30 exactly, a bounding rectangle, not the true bag footprint) and volume about 4,900 m3; built in 3.0 to 1.8 m of water below chart datum (= lowest astronomical tide) with the shallowest contour at 0.0 m below chart datum (reef as shallow as possible without emerging except at extreme low tide), on a thin sand layer over rock strata, no excavation [R18, printed pp. 3-4]. Designed for a right-hand wave 1.8-2.5 m high, rideable for about 100 m [R2][R3]. SIZE CONFLICT RESOLVED 2026-10-13: 99 x 30 m [R18] is the same design as Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.65): 30 m (longshore) x 100 m (cross-shore), depth 1.8-3.0 m, ~300 m offshore, 'at LAT' [R14]. The '90 m long x 20 m wide' of [R1][R2] (also repeated by SurferToday per earlier notes) is the earlier 2004 concept (bags 1.5-2 m high 'covering an area around 90m long and 20m wide', slight hook; Opunake Artificial Reef Committee chairman D. Lusk, The Daily News, 11 June 2004) [R19]; it is superseded by the consent-stage design and is no longer used as the reef's size. POSITION FOUND 2026-10-13: the reef lies inside the area Coastal Permit 6376-1 (31 May 2005) lets the Trust occupy: a 189 x 94 m rectangle (17,726 m2) with corners published as Taranaki local circuit grid co-ordinates (TRC 2009 Appendix I, PDF p.39) = centre -39.4594, 173.8516 (NZGD2000), long axis bearing 63 deg; where the 99 x 30 m reef sits inside it is unknown (+-47 m along, +-32 m across) [R18, R20; 07_scale/shapes/opunake-reef/consent_georef.json]. TRC Figure 1 (printed p.3) shows the same rectangle as 'Proposed location of surf reef'. Volume: design volume 4,800 m3 (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.3) [R13] agrees with TRC's 4,900 m3 within 2 percent; about 1,400 m3 was still needed to reach design crest height (p.3-4) and no funds were committed; last construction work May 2008 [R13]. 27 geo-textile bags were in place as of April 2008 [R18]. Rendle thesis Table 2.1 [R15] lists Opunake at 4,800 m3 of sand-filled containers, total cost A$760,000 (as printed; exchange rate 05/05/2011), construction start 2006, 'not officially completed' - agrees with design volume [R13], differs from NZ$1.1M-1.7M+ in [R1][R2] (different basis; both kept). No source found (papers/, web search 2026-10-10) gives a plan drawing, coordinates, bearing or crest depth with datum (negative search result of this project, 07_scale/shapes/opunake-reef/HANDOFF.md section 1). The monitoring report 'Opunake Artificial Reef Monitoring Programme 2005-2009', Taranaki Regional Council Technical Report 2009-33 (cited in [R14] and [R15]) was supplied by Lior and read 2026-10-13: [R18]. Shape/3D model: none. The reef's own plan shape is still not drawn: no source gives the bag layout, per-bag levels or an as-built survey, and the reef is not visible on LINZ 2011-12 or Esri imagery (07_scale/shapes/opunake-reef/FEASIBILITY.md).
cost: North reef costed at ~NZ$1.3 million before construction [R3]; council actually allocated NZ$1.1 million [R2]; spending had exceeded NZ$1.7 million by 2009 with a further NZ$400,000 sought [R1][R2]; council separately wrote off a NZ$400,000 loan to the Trust in 2011 [R2] Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): no fixed price; costs approaching twice the original estimate [R13]. Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.4): A$0.93 M in 2013 dollars, A$274 per m3, implying about 3,400 m3 built (design 4,800 minus 1,400 shortfall) [R14]. Council decision to fund NZ$1.1 million: 10 June 2004, reported 11 June 2004 [R19]. Consent bond NZ$50,000 on commencement of construction, guaranteed by the council (consent 6377-1 condition 18; TRC Table 3) [R18].
cost_usd_approx: No sourced USD conversion found in any reference; a rough unsourced conversion at ~0.65 NZD:USD puts the ~NZ$1.7m spend at roughly US$1.1m — Claude's own estimate, not a citable fact ASSUMPTION A1: exchange rate 0.65 NZD:USD is the agent's recollection, not from a source (replace with the RBNZ historical rate for 2009); effect about +-10 % on US$1.1 M.
financed_by: South Taranaki District Council (initial NZ$1.1M allocation plus a later NZ$400,000 loan) and the Opunake Artificial Surf Reef Trust, a local community trust [R1][R2]
motivation: Tourism and economic development for a declining South Taranaki town, via more frequent good surfing conditions; explicitly not a coastal-protection project [R2][R3]
designer: Dr Kerry Black / Artificial Surf Reefs (ASR) Ltd, Raglan, NZ, with surf-science design input from ASR co-founder Shaw Mead before he left the company in 2011 [R1][R2][R3][R5]
contractor: ASR Ltd (Raglan, NZ) — no separate named construction contractor found [R2][R3]
status_now: Failed: never produced the promised rideable waves [R1]. The Trust sued ASR in 2011; the council wrote off its debt as unrecoverable; ASR itself was liquidated in 2012 [R2]. No source found reports formal removal or dismantling of the structure [R1][R2] Decision: verdict 'failed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source, because the reef never produced the promised waves [R1], construction was never completed [R13][R14] (Blacka Table 4.1: surfing 'No (construction incomplete)'), the Trust sued ASR and the council wrote off its debt [R2]. Counter-view kept: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3-4) say the most complete inside section gives good-quality waves [R13]. Sept 2009 (TRC) [R18]: reef 'basically in place' (27 bags), not complete; no post-construction survey or dive-survey result found.
hover_text: A ~99x30x3.5 m (design) submerged sand-bag reef off Opunake Beach, Taranaki, planned for ~NZ$1.3 million from 2006 but ending up costing over NZ$1.7 million by 2009 [R1][R2][R3] — it never produced the rideable waves it was designed for, and the project ended in litigation, a written-off council loan, and the designer's liquidation in 2012 [R1][R2].
design_as_planned: Two reefs were planned: a cheaper north reef (built first) costed at ~NZ$1.3 million [R3], designed (consent stage) as a 99 x 30 x 3.5 m reef of about 4,900 m3 [R18] (the 2004 concept was ~90 x 20 m with bags 1.5-2 m high [R19]) for a fast hollow right-hand wave 1.8-2.5 m high rideable for ~100 m [R2][R3][R18]; and a larger, never-built south reef meant to deliver a 200 m ride on waves up to 3.6 m high [R3]. ASR tested the design in a small-scale wave pool at its Raglan facility [R2]. Kerry Black publicly expected the north reef to be finished within about two months of construction starting [R2][R3]. Design history [R18, printed pp. 2-3]: the idea was first pursued in 1998 by Mr Eddie Klaassen and future Trust members; Dr Kerry Black did a site-selection study (sites within 10 km of the town; best sites in Opunake Bay); ASR Ltd's Phase I feasibility study (2001, computer modelling and data collection) found two satisfactory positions, north and south sides of the bay; after consultation the north side was chosen and ASR did the Phase II detailed design and environmental studies for the consents. The position was set from bathymetry, rock and sand cover, aerial photographs, video and visual observations, numerical modelling and wave-angle measurements. Built from large sand-filled geo-textile containers made to reproduce the designed profile, not fixed to the seabed (stability from weight and friction). Black and Mead (2006) 'Opunake Reef Construction Manual' (ASR) is cited by TRC (printed p.20), not found online.
as_built_vs_design: Only the cheaper north reef was ever attempted; the south reef was never built [R2][R13][R14]. Construction, planned for ~2 months, instead dragged on for years: by 2009 all 27 geotextile bags were reportedly in place but still needed "fine tuning" (more sand, closing gaps between bags), while spending had already passed NZ$1.7 million against the NZ$1.1 million council allocation [R1][R2]. A 2009-10 proposal to cap the geo-containers with rock (est. NZ$150,000) was pledged by ASR's new part-owner Sealutions LLC as part of a sale agreement but was never honoured [R2]. In 2010 seabed changes were reported to be causing uneven performance across the reef [R2]. By August 2011 the council, Trust and ASR relationship had broken down entirely, ending in litigation [R2]. TRC 2009 (read 2026-10-13) [R18]: construction began early 2006, was halted by weather and the equipment being needed at Mount Maunganui, resumed over the next two summers (site sign: works February 2007 to May 200?, read as 2008); as of April 2008 27 bags were in place with fine-tuning planned for 2009/2010; the council still rated the Trust's environmental performance 'good' and noted no adverse effects (baseline kaimoana and intertidal surveys 2006-07; post-construction surveys to follow); the as-built confirmation and the position survey (+-5 m) required by consent 6377-1 conditions 9 and 10 were not yet due ('reef not yet complete', Table 3); the required signs at Opunake Beach were missing and TRC called the nearly finished reef 'already a potential hazard' for boating (printed p.15); TRC recommended a dive survey of the structure in 2009-10 (printed p.18) - its result was not found.
outcome: No source found gives a measured/instrumented surf-quality outcome for Opunake (no wave-height, peel-angle or ride-length monitoring data, unlike Narrowneck) — "not found" (negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement). Qualitatively, every source agrees the reef never produced the promised rideable waves; a 2021 investigative piece states flatly the reef "didn't produce the expected waves" [R1]. The reef did attract fish and other sea-life, but the structure itself began to break apart, with pieces washing ashore [R1]. No coastal-protection outcome is reported because none was designed in [R3]. No removal/dismantling is documented in any source found [R1][R2]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3-4) note the inside (most complete) section gives good-quality waves but the reef is widely considered a failure; predominant NW winds are mostly offshore and waves are pre-conditioned in the bay [R13]. This differs in tone from [R1] (reef 'didn't produce the expected waves'): sources disagree, both kept. Blacka Table 4.1 rates surfing 'No (construction incomplete)' [R14].
why_worked_or_failed: It failed. Contributing causes across sources: chronic under-budgeting and repeated funding shortfalls (the NZ$1.1-1.3M allocation proved far short of the NZ$1.7M+ actually spent, and later top-up requests of NZ$400,000, NZ$150,000 and NZ$133,000 were each unmet or only partly met) [R1][R2]; the intrinsic durability problem of sand-filled geotextile bags, which ASR co-founder Shaw Mead later called the technology's "fatal flaw" — a single torn bag loses sand and changes the whole structure's shape [R5]; seabed changes over time causing uneven performance across the reef by 2010 [R2]; and corporate instability at ASR (majority sale to Sealutions LLC, an unhonoured completion pledge, and ASR's own liquidation in 2012) that removed any prospect of finishing the fix [R1][R2]. Because the reef was designed purely for surfing with no coastal-protection goal, there was no secondary benefit to justify the sunk cost once the surf failed to materialise [R3].
unexpected_results: The reef attracted fish and other sea-life even as it failed to produce surf [R1]. Pieces of the failed structure washed ashore over time [R1], a pattern echoed more dramatically at the related Mount Maunganui and Boscombe ASR reefs [R1]. The dispute escalated beyond an engineering failure into litigation: the Trust sued ASR in 2011, and the council wrote off first a NZ$400,000 loan and then its whole claim as unrecoverable [R1][R2]. No source found documents fishing pressure, swimmer-safety/rip-current incidents, or tourism data specific to Opunake — "not found" [R1][R5].
could_be_better: ASR co-founder Shaw Mead concluded the geotextile-bag construction method itself was the core weakness and said it led him to shift subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to traditional rock construction [R5]; he separately called the sandbag approach "an evolutionary deadend" in an email to Newsroom [R1]. At Opunake specifically, ASR's own 2009-10 fix proposal was to cap the geo-containers with rock rather than keep tuning bags with sand, but the funding for that fix was never delivered [R2]. Surfrider Foundation CEO Jim Moriarty argued more broadly that ocean-based artificial-reef attempts as a class have "absolutely horrible" results and that effort should go into protecting natural breaks instead [R6]. NZ Surfing Magazine editor Cory Scott was blunter still: "not one artificial reef has created a wave of any quality, despite claims to the contrary" [R1]. Process-wise, the repeated pattern of underestimating both time (2 months expected; it ran years) and cost (three separate unmet top-up requests) suggests firmer contingency budgeting and a completion-guarantee contract with the builder would have been needed to finish the job at all [R1][R2].
relevance_to_israel: Tide range is the biggest physical contrast: Opunake's open New Zealand coast shows a sample tidal range on the order of ~2.5 m (high 2.94 m / low 0.47 m, one sample day, datum not stated) [R7] and more than 3.0 m according to Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.3) [R14], versus well under half a metre at Haifa on Israel's virtually tideless Mediterranean coast (~0.36-0.40 m high / ~0.00-0.07 m low) [R12]. A geotextile-bag reef at Opunake has to keep working across that ~2.5 m swing in water depth every tide cycle — a substantially harder crest-depth design problem than any Israeli Mediterranean site would present, which is a point in Israel's favour for a similar reef proposal (INFERENCE of this card's author; the ~2.5 m swing is DERIVED as 2.94 m - 0.47 m = 2.47 m from one sample day [R7], Blacka's spring range is >3.0 m [R14]). However, the dominant documented failure modes at Opunake — chronic under-budgeting, repeated shortfalls in "finishing" funding, corporate instability at the design/construction firm, and the durability problem of sand-filled geotextile bags (tear -> sand loss -> shape change -> wave-quality loss) [R1][R2][R5] — are not tide-dependent and would transfer directly to any Israeli geotextile-bag project, including the Ashkelon geotube project already logged in this project's master list, which itself suffered partial construction failure (15 of 48 geotubes destroyed before the layout was completed) and higher-than-expected maintenance costs (Bar, D. and Drimer, N. (2023), J. Mar. Sci. Eng. 11, 236, https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse11020236, as summarised in 01_source_notes/jmse2023_bar_drimer_paper.md and 02_research/00_master_list.md; paper's own figures not re-checked in this audit). The clearest transferable lesson is financial and material: secure full contingency funding and a completion-guarantee contract before committing to a geotextile-bag structure, and weigh rock-based construction (which ASR's own co-founder ultimately endorsed over bags) given the technology's poor track record on sand-bag durability [R1][R2][R5][R7][R12]. Design crest level [R18]: the shallowest contour was set at 0.0 m below chart datum (= lowest astronomical tide), i.e. as shallow as possible without emerging except at extreme low tide, in a 3 m or larger tidal range; for Haifa's small tide the equivalent crest depth would be set relative to local mean sea level, not chart datum (project reasoning, not a source statement).
